claims.text: The eutectic high-entropy alloy has a fine lamellar microstructure of alternating soft FCC and hard BCC phases.
Galvanic coupling at FCC/BCC phase boundaries drives the accelerated coupled degradation.
The FCC and BCC phases have differing oxidation kinetics at elevated temperature.
Differential oxidation of the phases produces non-uniform oxide scales along phase boundaries.
The resulting oxide scales are brittle.
Mechanical sliding periodically spalls or removes the oxide scales.
Oxide removal exposes fresh alloy surfaces that form local galvanic cells and corrode rapidly.
Galvanically accelerated corrosion further weakens the alloy structure.
Corrosion-induced weakening increases susceptibility to mechanical damage, creating a self-reinforcing degradation cycle.
The multiphase eutectic alloy will have greater total degradation than a compositionally matched homogeneous single-phase alloy.
The multiphase eutectic alloy will have a higher corrosion rate than the single-phase baseline because of galvanic effects.
The multiphase eutectic alloy will have a higher wear rate than the single-phase baseline because brittle oxide scales are removed.
The multiphase alloy will exhibit elevated mass loss.
The multiphase alloy will exhibit deeper wear tracks and evidence of oxide spallation.
Corrosion will be more localized at phase boundaries.
The qualitative synergy between wear and corrosion is supported by the cited evidence.
The proposed mechanism is scoped to concurrent mechanical sliding and an oxidizing, corrosive environment above approximately 700°C.
A compositionally matched homogeneous single-phase alloy without distinct phase boundaries is the proposed control.
The relative quantitative contributions of galvanic corrosion and mechanical oxide spallation are uncertain.
Detectable local electrochemical-potential differences near phase boundaries are expected if galvanic coupling is active.
